records.name: Bayern
records.summary:
Since 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German has been prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration in Bavaria, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 through a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities. Coverage notes critics dismissing the measure as symbol politics while recording its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom a visitor might deal with.

Bavaria is also a partner — with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt — in a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change: an organised state-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter, which critics see as restricting how trans and intersex people use the right.

records.name: Berlin
records.summary:
Germany's Pride movement faces a documented rise in attacks: the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-motivated attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including a boiling-water attack, and runs a €100,000 support fund weighted to eastern Germany. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day, with hundreds of thousands expected, Berlin's organisers nonetheless urged participants to 'be vigilant'.

The reporting also situates the capital: Maneo, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades like Berlin's had not been specifically threatened — smaller towns are hardest to police — while everyday hostility still surfaces: one Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in eighteen months.

records.name: Brandenburg
records.summary:
In Cottbus on 20 October 2025, a rubbish container was set alight against the façade of the 'Regenbogenkombinat' queer cultural centre during CSD week; the fire was out in about fifteen minutes and nobody was hurt, but state security (Staatsschutz) took over the arson investigation and a political motive cannot be excluded — local initiatives call it an attempted firebombing, and the attack sits among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the city.

The subsequent Cottbus CSD — the 17th edition, under the motto 'Vereint in Frieden und Vielfalt' — ran with a large police presence against two registered far-right counter-demonstrations, one organised by 'Deutsche Jugend voran', and proceeded without major disruption. The local queer community describes itself as unusually watchful: repeated physical pressure on infrastructure, met by a functioning protective response.

records.name: Hessen
records.summary:
A Hessen Landtag small inquiry with the Interior Minister's answer (April 2025) records police-registered queer-hostile offences rising from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024 — a year-on-year jump of 52 that the minister's reply calls alarming.

The trend must be read with the federal BKA's own caveat: its situation report on LSBTIQ* security introduced a new reporting category that makes state-by-state comparison possible but warns that classification changes can inflate registered counts, so rises may partly reflect better recording rather than a sharper danger. The same answer notes the 2010-established network of LSBTIQ* liaison officers in every police headquarters, governed by a standing framework concept — an institutional response in place while the statistics remain ambiguous.

records.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
records.summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three Länder — with Sachsen and Thüringen — that brought a Bundesrat initiative (reported June 2026) to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act on legal gender change, proposing an 'abuse review' mechanism with objective, documentable grounds for registry-office intervention. The trigger cited is the 'Fall Liebich' — a convicted far-right extremist whose legal gender was changed after sentencing.

The initiative is an attempt, not a change: it is backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, and runs against a scheduled federal evaluation of the SBGG that the family ministry is conducting and whose SPD-led ministries consider the existing law sufficient. No standing administrative ban or documented street-attack pattern specific to this state was identified in the research pass.

records.name: Thüringen
records.summary:
Thüringen's Landtag exhibits formal, multi-layered hostility to gender policy: an AfD fraction motion demands consistent implementation of a ban on gender-inclusive language in Thuringian schools, asserting schools must not be "a socio-political experimental field"; a draft law titled "Thüringer Gesetz zur Beendigung gleichstellungspolitischer Maßnahmen" proposes to dismantle the Land's existing equality-policy machinery, arguing that current law "regularly violates the principle of equal opportunity." Thüringen is also a partner in the Sachsen/Sachsen-Anhalt June 2026 Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal SBGG. The dossier characterises the parliament as "formally hostile to gender policy."

National score is 0.71. Thüringen sits 0.06 below: the equality-dismantling bill is the most consequential institutional signal in this dossier for a visitor — if enacted, a trans person reporting an incident would find no Land-level equality apparatus. The gender-language motion compounds this at the administrative interface. Compared to Sachsen-Anhalt (0.68), Thüringen goes beyond tightening one federal law to actively removing the entire state equality framework; compared to Brandenburg (0.66), the threat is legislative and institutional rather than physical but arguably more pervasive for a visitor's access to recourse. Compared to Bayern (0.67), Thüringen's hostility extends to dismantling protection machinery rather than restricting expression vocabulary.

records.name: Wales
records.summary:
Wales's devolved administration has publicly maintained its LGBTQ+ Action Plan through the UK's post-judgment years: the plan's standing update page was issued answering the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025, with a dedicated young-people's edition posted January 2026.

Its 'Rights, Respect, Equality' statutory school guidance (consultation May 2025) obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on the grounds of sex, gender reassignment and sexual orientation, with incident recording and monitoring and a parental escalation route. The practical facility rules set state-wide are unchanged here, but the visible institutional commitment — maintained action plan, statutory recording duties — is an official posture of inclusion at a national moment of rollback.

records.name: Northern Ireland
records.summary:
Northern Ireland carries three sub-national negatives absent elsewhere in the UK: Education Minister Paul Givan ordered the 2019 transgender-pupils guidance withdrawn from the Education Authority website in September 2025 after the FWS ruling, calling it "unlawful and flawed" and a product of "activist campaigns"; the Justice Minister's attempt to include transgender people as a protected group in hate-crime sentencing reform was stalled (reported DUP obstruction); and the Rainbow Project records a pattern of paramilitary-flavoured anti-LGB&T violence including a pipe bomb thrown through the home of a trans woman in Derry/Londonderry described by PSNI as a "sectarian hate crime," a 2019 Belfast city-centre assault hospitalising a gay man, and an average of ~290 anti-LGB&T incidents per year (2013–2017) with rising transgender-identity strand counts to September 2025.

Counter-balancing: PSNI/NISRA track a separate "transgender identity" category (unlike England and Wales), evidencing institutional recognition; the Health Minister publicly defended gender-identity service funding (£800k+ uplift) against DUP/TUV criticism, showing the executive is split rather than uniformly hostile. No criminal ban on expression or police-enforced facility prohibition exists — the risk mechanism mirrors the national EHRC code (service refusal by staff) plus street-level violence.
